structure.title: Prudential disclosures on environmental, social and governance risks
structure.heading: 7. Prudential disclosures on environmental, social and governance risks
structure.start_phrase: Sustainability for BBVA means “helping our customers in the transition to a sustainable future” by fostering environmental protection, economic growth and social development.
structure.summary: This section of the Pillar 3 2024 report presents prudential disclosures on ESG risks. It introduces the governance model for sustainability, emphasizing sustainability as a strategic priority and outlining the applicable regulatory framework. It then covers how environmental, social, and governance risks are managed: for environmental and social risks, it describes strategy and business processes alongside risk management practices; for governance risk, it focuses on risk management. Overall, it explains how ESG considerations are integrated into governance, strategy, and risk management.

structure.title: Introduction and governance model
structure.heading: 7.1. Introduction and governance model
structure.start_phrase: Sustainability for BBVA means “helping our customers in the transition to a sustainable future” by fostering environmental protection, economic growth and social development.
structure.summary:
- Sets sustainability as a strategic priority for BBVA, defined as helping customers transition to a sustainable future while fostering environmental protection, economic growth, and social development.
- Explains key drivers: climate change’s long-term investment needs, stress on natural capital (water, crops, raw materials), and persistent inequalities that may be worsened by decarbonization and ecosystem loss.
- Details BBVA’s role via the ESG dimensions:
  - Environmental: addressing climate and natural capital challenges; supporting client transition through products and services.
  - Social: promoting inclusive growth through its core business, financial inclusion (“bankarization”), financial literacy, and inclusive infrastructure; complemented by responsible practices and philanthropy.
  - Governance: ensuring compliance, responsible conduct, and strong ethical standards; defining governance frameworks and policies for sustainability.
- Outlines the regulatory framework for ESG risk disclosures:
  - European Banking Authority Implementing Technical Standards (ITS) on ESG risk disclosures under Pillar 3, incorporated via Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2022/2453 amending Regulation (EU) 2021/637.
  - Spanish Law 7/2021 on climate change and energy transition: mandates annual reporting on the financial impact of climate-related risks (including transition risks) and the measures taken, and requires publication from 2023 of Paris-aligned decarbonization targets for loan and investment portfolios.

structure.title: Sustainability as a strategic priority
structure.heading: 7.1.1. Sustainability as a strategic priority
structure.start_phrase:
Sustainability for BBVA means “helping our customers in 
the transition to a sustainable future” by fostering 
environmental protection, economic growth and social 
development.
structure.summary:
- Establishes BBVA’s view of sustainability as a strategic priority: helping customers transition to a sustainable future while fostering environmental protection, economic growth, and social development, leveraging the banking sector’s multiplier effect.
- Highlights key context and challenges: climate change’s long-term investment needs; growing stress on natural capital (water, crops, raw materials); and persistent inequalities that could worsen during decarbonization—underscoring banks’ role in financial inclusion, literacy, and inclusive infrastructure.
- Outlines the ESG pillars:
  - Environmental: need for collective action; inclusion of natural capital; BBVA supports client transition via products and services.
  - Social: promotion of inclusive growth benefiting vulnerable segments through core business, responsible practices, and philanthropic initiatives.
  - Governance: strict legal compliance and ethical standards; focus on business conduct, policies, and sustainability governance frameworks.
- Summarizes regulatory framework for disclosures:
  - EBA Implementing Technical Standards (ITS) on ESG risks for Pillar 3, finalized Jan 24, 2022, incorporated via Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2022/2453 amending Implementing Regulation (EU) 2021/637.
  - Spanish Law 7/2021 on climate change and energy transition: mandates annual reporting on financial impacts of climate risks (including transition risks) and adopted measures, and requires publication (from 2023) of Paris-aligned decarbonization targets for loan and investment portfolios.
- Positions the content within BBVA’s Pillar 3 2024 prudential ESG risk disclosures (Section 7: Introduction and governance model).

structure.title: Regulatory framework
structure.heading: 7.1.2. Regulatory framework
structure.start_phrase:
On January 24, 2022, the European Banking Authority 
published its final draft implementing technical 
standards (“ITS”), amending the CRR on Pillar 3 
disclosures relating to environmental, social and 
governance (“ESG”) risks.
structure.summary:
- BBVA positions sustainability as a core strategic priority focused on helping clients transition to a sustainable future, emphasizing environmental protection, inclusive economic growth, and social development.
- Environmental focus includes addressing climate change and natural capital pressures (water, crops, raw materials) through products and services that support client transition.
- Social focus centers on inclusive growth via financial inclusion (“bankarization”), financial literacy, and support for inclusive infrastructure (health, education, communications), alongside responsible practices and philanthropic initiatives.
- Governance focus underscores strict legal compliance, ethical conduct, and alignment of sustainability with business conduct, policies, and regulatory frameworks.
- Regulatory framework highlights EBA Pillar 3 Implementing Technical Standards for ESG risk disclosures (EU 2022/2453) and Spain’s Law 7/2021, requiring annual reporting on climate-related financial risks, transition risks, and publication of portfolio decarbonization targets; disclosures span governance, strategy, impacts, risk management, and metrics/targets (including Scope 1–3).
- Governance model integrates ESG risk oversight within BBVA’s Corporate Governance System, led by the Board of Directors under established bylaws and regulations (e.g., Article 17), covering strategy, budget, Risk Appetite Framework, and general policies.
- Decision-making process flows from executive areas to corporate bodies with complete and consistent reporting, active management of conflicts of interest, and iterative debate to align with corporate interest and purpose.
- Supervision and Control Model ensures execution, monitoring, and continuous oversight of decisions and policies, with ESG governance embedded across structures and processes.

structure.title: Governance model
structure.heading: 7.1.3. Governance model
structure.start_phrase:
BBVA has a corporate governance system, comprising a 
set of principles, rules and mechanisms that integrate 
and regulate the structures and operation of its 
corporate bodies (hereinafter, the "System" or the 
"Corporate Governance System").
structure.summary:
- Scope and reporting framework: Sets out climate-related reporting criteria across governance, strategy, impacts, risk management, and metrics/goals, including Scope 1–3 GHG and reduction approach, aligned with Article 449 bis CRR templates.

- Corporate governance model: Describes BBVA’s Corporate Governance System, Board of Directors’ powers (per Bylaws and Article 17 of its Regulations), decision-making, supervision and control processes, and a comprehensive reporting model ensuring complete, integrated, adequate and consistent information, with committee support and access to external experts.

- Sustainability governance at Board level: Sustainability is a strategic priority embedded in the 2019–2024 Strategic Plan and the General Sustainability Policy. ESG factors are integrated into the Strategic Plan, Budget (annual targets), and Risk Appetite Framework (including HTR metrics and portfolio decarbonization). Board committees’ ESG roles:
  - Executive Committee (CDP): strategy, objectives, and implementation follow-up.
  - Risk & Compliance: integration of sustainability in financial/non-financial risk management.
  - Audit: oversight of sustainability-related public information.
  - Appointments & Corporate Governance: Board composition skills on sustainability and CG system effectiveness.
  - Remuneration: sustainability-linked indicators in incentives.
  - Technology & Cybersecurity: tech strategy and cybersecurity oversight.

- Executive-level integration: Establishes a Global Sustainability Area reporting to the CEO (business) and Chair (transformation/strategy), with cross-cutting responsibility to embed sustainability in all areas. Includes:
  - A Group-wide sustainability expert network across business and control functions.
  - Sustainability Alignment Steering Group (SASG) to propose/monitor sectoral alignment objectives, with quarterly executive reviews and periodic Board reporting.
  - ESG Reporting Committee to coordinate quality and consistency of public ESG disclosures.
  - Integration into management reporting and decision-making (e.g., profitability and sustainable business KPIs in Spain).
  - Single Development Agenda (SDA) governance of sustainability projects (€52.5m in 2024) spanning product transformation, risk/process adaptation to physical/transition risks, decarbonization, inclusive growth, ESG reporting, and data/technology for sustainability indicators.

- ESG risk processes in wholesale banking: Procedure for environmental and social disputes; CEOG oversees client engagement and compliance with the Environmental & Social Framework and Equator Principles; New Business Committee incorporates ESG risk into transaction approvals; Sustainable Finance CIB team and Reputation Holding unit escalate reputational/ESG analyses to senior fora. New Wholesale and Sustainability Committee (Dec 2024) is the main body for integrating climate/environmental risks into risk management (taxonomies, emissions methodologies for RAF metrics, tool approval, model build/buy decisions, and feedback on E&S Framework revisions).

- Board activities and oversight cadence: Board approved the General Sustainability Policy (revised 2022), a €300bn 2018–2025 sustainable business channeling target, portfolio decarbonization targets toward net zero by 2050, and €550m community investment. In 2024, the Board received regular Sustainability reports; inclusive growth was reported three times to the Board and twice to the CDP. Business and global areas routinely report sustainability initiatives, projects and resourcing.

- Remuneration aligned to ESG: Directors’ Remuneration Policy (approved March 17, 2023 for 2023–2026) includes annual short-term and multi-year long-term incentives with financial and non-financial metrics. 2024 indicators include:
  - Short-term: profit, RORC, efficiency; NPS, target customers, and sustainable business channeling.
  - Long-term: TBV per share, relative TSR; portfolio decarbonization and women in management.
  - Sustainability-linked indicators account for 32.8% of target annual variable remuneration; decarbonization has an explicit weighting and disclosed contribution to total compensation.

- People, conduct, and labor standards: Commits to employee engagement and diversity (women in management at 35.4% in 2024; target 36.8% by 2026). Gender-neutral remuneration policies with an adjusted median salary gap of 0.6% in 2024. Code of Conduct and mandatory ethics/compliance training (including anti-corruption). Labor rights governed by local laws, sectoral and union agreements, with local/global labor relations teams; transparent communication of working conditions via internal channels.

- Cross-references: Notes that detailed strategies and risk management for environmental, social, and governance risks are further developed in sections 7.2 (Environmental), 7.3 (Social), and 7.4 (Governance).

structure.title: Environmental Risk
structure.heading: 7.2. Environmental Risk
structure.start_phrase:
BBVA has made sustainability one of its six strategic
priorities, focusing on the fight against climate change,
the protection of natural capital, and inclusive growth.
structure.summary:
- Section outlines BBVA’s environmental risk approach within its sustainability strategy, under Pillar 3 (Article 449 bis CRR), focusing on strategy and business processes.
- BBVA names sustainability as a strategic priority centered on climate action, natural capital protection, and inclusive growth.
- Two overarching objectives:
  1) Grow sustainable business: initial goal to channel EUR 300bn (2018–2025) surpassed at EUR 304bn by 31 Dec 2024; about EUR 99bn channeled in 2024; new target of EUR 700bn for 2025–2029.
  2) Achieve Net Zero by 2050 via sectoral decarbonization plans with 2030 interim targets.
- 2024 sustainable financing included over EUR 77bn directed to industrial electrification, energy efficiency, renewable energy projects, solar self-consumption, and transformation of transport and logistics.
- Interim 2030 decarbonization targets cover oil & gas (upstream), power generation, autos, steel, cement, thermal coal mining, aviation, shipping; 2024 additions include aluminum (primary manufacturing) and real estate (commercial and residential in Spain).
- Targets are set using alignment methodologies to link financial flows to emissions reductions and to guide sectoral plans, client engagement, risk management, and opportunity capture; clients’ transition plans are assessed.
- Portfolio measurement notes: high-emission sector exposure is evaluated across both drawn and undrawn products (loans, RCFs, guarantees, ECA lines, etc.); customers “actively managing their transition” are identified via internal tools (e.g., Transition Risk Indicator—TRi) considering targets, levers, and committed investments.

structure.title: Strategy and business processes
structure.heading: 7.2.1. Strategy and business processes
structure.start_phrase: BBVA has made sustainability one of its six strategic priorities, focusing on the fight against climate change, the protection of natural capital, and inclusive growth.
structure.summary:
- BBVA positions sustainability as a core strategic priority, centered on combating climate change, protecting natural capital, and promoting inclusive growth.
- Two main goals guide the strategy: (1) foster sustainable business, and (2) reach net-zero emissions by 2050 through sectoral decarbonization plans.
- Sustainable business targets and progress:
  - 2018–2025 target of EUR 300 billion was surpassed (EUR 304 billion by Dec-2024); EUR 99 billion channeled in 2024 (+42% vs 2023).
  - New 2025–2029 target: EUR 700 billion.
  - In 2024, >EUR 77 billion was directed to climate action, supporting electrification, efficiency, renewables, self-consumption, and low‑carbon transport/logistics.
- Net-zero and 2030 interim targets:
  - Sector coverage includes oil & gas (upstream), power generation, autos, cement, steel, coal, aviation, shipping, and since 2024, aluminum (global) and real estate (commercial and residential in Spain).
  - Coal phase-out: by 2030 in developed countries and 2040 globally.
  - Alignment methodologies include PACTA (sector intensity), PCAF (financed emissions), and benchmarks such as IEA NZE 2050, ISF NZ, IMO strategy; real estate aligned to Spain’s NECP.
  - Reported portfolio metrics and “distance to scenario” for key sectors; oil & gas financed emissions down from 14 MtCO2e (2021) to 10.5 Mt (2024), targeting -30% by 2030.
  - Shipping alignment updated to IMO’s higher-ambition path; 2024 deltas at -7.49% (minimum) and -2.99% (effort trajectory).
- Integration into business and financial planning:
  - Sustainability embedded in product development across wholesale, corporate, and retail segments; continuous client dialogue.
  - Regular management reporting on sustainable business channeling, profitability, penetration, and P&L/balance metrics, with planned geographic expansion of sustainability reporting.
- Criteria for classifying sustainable business:
  - Internal standards inspired by the EU Taxonomy and adapted to non‑EU contexts; CIB Sustainable Products Framework with external opinion; use of ICMA/LMA principles for use‑of‑proceeds and sustainability‑linked instruments; consideration of SFDR and other regulations.
  - Clear distinction between BBVA’s internal “channeling” metric and EU Taxonomy regulatory metrics.
- Sector transition plans and management tools:
  - Transition plans define commercial strategy, portfolio appetite, monitoring, and risk mitigation per sector.
  - Tools include the Transition Risk Indicator (TRi), Sustainability Client Toolkit, sector plan dashboards (PACTA outputs), and a “What if” simulator to assess transaction impacts on client and portfolio decarbonization paths.
- Client engagement and support:
  - Formalized customer support plans (2024) to advise on and monitor client transition strategies; actions range from tailored advisory to underweighting growth or orderly exit if plans underperform.
  - Deep sectoral advisory (e.g., O&G, power, autos, cement, steel, chemicals, infrastructure, food & bev, tech/pharma) and themes (cleantech, biodiversity, carbon markets, nature-based solutions, Scope 3 and supply chain).
  - Broad SME support through branches/digital channels and project consulting (efficiency, renewables, CCUS, mobility, batteries, hydrogen, biofuels, inclusive growth).
- Governance and incentives:
  - Sustainability Alignment Steering Group (SASG) oversees targets, progress, plans, and tool deployment.
  - Reinforced sector coverage model for wholesale clients with global sector leads (energy; industry/transport; infrastructure/construction; plus consumer/retail/healthcare, TMT, FIs, sponsors).
  - Long-term incentives linked to decarbonization performance in priority sectors.
- EU Taxonomy (Article 8) disclosures:
  - Explanation of eligibility vs alignment, DNSH and Minimum Social Safeguards, and data dependencies on NFRD reporters.
  - GAR limitations highlighted (e.g., exclusions of non‑NFRD, non‑EU exposures from numerator), creating structural differences across banks.
  - Reported KPIs: GAR stock 0.57% (coverage 65.36%) and GAR flow 0.50% (coverage 23.84%); detailed breakdowns of covered assets, eligible/aligned shares across counterparties and products.
- Other climate mitigation actions not covered by EU Taxonomy:
  - Outstanding exposures to green/sustainable/sustainability‑linked bonds and loans under market standards (outside EU Taxonomy alignment), including real estate and renovation loans; qualitative criteria and focus on transition and physical risk mitigation noted.
- Risk framework integration (intro to section 7.2.2):
  - Climate and environmental risks are embedded across the risk management cycle to support BBVA’s low‑carbon transition strategy and net‑zero ambition.

structure.title: Risk Management
structure.heading: 7.2.2. Risk Management
structure.start_phrase:
Managing climate and environmental risk factors is key 
to implementing BBVA's strategy, which is based on 
managing risks appropriately, helping the transition to a 
low-carbon economy and meeting the ambition of having 
net-zero carbon emissions by 2050.
structure.summary:
- Client engagement on ESG: BBVA advises wholesale, business and SME clients on tailored sustainability strategies by sector and geography; covers regulation, disclosure, market developments, ESG ratings; provides sector-specialized advice (e.g., oil & gas, power, autos, cement, chemicals, mining, infrastructure, food/bev, pharma/tech) aligned with Paris and energy transition roadmaps; supports Scope 3 and supplier footprint analysis; offers sustainable finance products (bonds, loans, transactional banking) and project consulting (energy efficiency, renewables, CCUS, mobility, batteries, green H2, biofuels, inclusive growth). Expanded specialist teams across geographies and digital/branch channels for SMEs.

- Integration of climate and environmental (C&E) risks into risk framework: Adoption of tiered risk taxonomies; mapping climate transition and physical drivers to traditional prudential risks (credit, market, liquidity, operational, reputational, business/strategy, real estate).

- Risk identification and assessment: Global Risk Assessment updated at least semiannually; since 2024, enhanced quantitative Climate Risk Assessment with metrics for transition and physical risks, including water stress; uses NGFS transition scenarios and IPCC-based physical scenarios (SSP2-4.5/SSP3-7.0); assessed across time horizons (short, medium, long) and major geographies.

- 2024 risk conclusions: Main vulnerabilities in credit portfolios medium/long term; transition risk materializes earlier in Spain (EU policy pace); physical risk deterioration over time from more frequent/severe events; low impact on liquidity and market risk; operational risk medium in Spain, low elsewhere; greenwashing probability relatively higher short term.

- Scenario analysis and stress testing: Climate integrated into baseline and high-loss risk scenarios for ICAAP; physical risk events (droughts) for Spain and Mexico included; transition shock via green-asset bubble burst added; progressing to sectoral and client/location-level modeling; participated in EBA’s “One‑off Fit‑for‑55” supervisory exercise—key finding: transition risks alone not systemically destabilizing but amplify losses with macro shocks.

- Transition risk management: Internal sector categorization of High Transition Risk (HTR) sectors; 11.7% of wholesale exposure (5.9% of Group EAD) in HTR; development and rollout of Transition Risk Indicator (TRi) across sectors to assess exposure and credibility/implementation of decarbonization plans; TRi used for client segmentation and risk policies.

- Financed emissions (Scope 3 Cat. 15): PCAF methodology applied across lending (corporates, project finance, CRE, mortgages, auto) and ex‑lending (FI and equity) in main geographies; 2024 perimeter expanded to Turkey and Argentina plus ex‑lending; financed emissions by asset types and geography disclosed; like‑for‑like perimeter shows 15.3% reduction; Group intensity 690 tCO2e/€M; data quality scoring per PCAF; acknowledges future volatility with factor updates and more client-reported data.

- EU Paris-aligned Benchmarks exclusions: Identification methodology based on external ESG data and NACE mapping for coal, oil, gas, and high‑intensity power generation thresholds; exposure to top 20 global carbon-intensive firms limited (7 clients; €1,188m; 0.23% of non‑financial exposure; short WAM).

- Mortgages and energy efficiency: EPC data collection and modeling across Spain, Turkey, Mexico, Peru; integration of EPC into mortgage origination, pricing incentives (e.g., “Hipoteca Casa Eficiente” for A/B-rated homes), and financing for energy-efficiency upgrades; plans to refresh EPC data from official sources; greenwashing prevention program embedded in non‑financial risk.

- Physical risk framework: Internal taxonomy of hazards (cyclones, heat waves, wildfires, river/coastal floods, drought); threat–exposure–vulnerability approach; collateral-level physical risk scoring under SSP2-4.5; mapping of asset locations underway; portfolio exposure breakdown shows shares of loans/mortgages exposed to physical risk; sectoral exposure and maturity distribution disclosed.

- Natural capital risk: Internal taxonomy built on ENCORE and aligned with SBTN/TNFD LEAP; assesses sector impacts/dependencies on ecosystem services (water, land use, pollution, waste, biodiversity); 34% of wholesale EAD sensitive to natural capital risk; prioritized sectors include agriculture, food/bev, paper/forestry, traditional power, construction, integrated oil & gas/utilities, transport infrastructure, mining, metals, E&P; integration into Sector Action Frameworks and KYC; onboarding of providers to geolocate client assets.

- Risk appetite and strategic resilience: RAF sets Group/geography thresholds for HTR exposure and a new indicator for sector decarbonization target compliance; “High Market Misalignment” client metric monitors emission-intensity outliers vs IEA NZE trajectories; moving to tighter appetite by TRi bands; developing physical-risk and financed-emissions monitoring; sector frameworks define client admission, mitigation, and growth policies; retail frameworks embed EPC+LTV origination limits; differentiated pricing for green products (mortgages and EVs).

- Policies, underwriting, and tools: ESG risk integrated into wholesale admission and annual reviews (Environmental & Social Framework, TRi results, sector guidelines, alignment plans, controversies); dedicated ESG risk teams support analysts; Client Sustainability Toolkit aggregates internal/external data (emissions, targets, ratings, controversies, water use, alignment, financed emissions, TRi); ~3,000 corporate clients assessed.

- Strategy resilience actions: TCFD-aligned scenario analysis indicates immaterial impacts to date with caveats on data/methods; adverse stress test of exiting selected clients underperforming on support plans shows strategy remains sound; climate risks embedded across risk cycle, ICAAP, provisions, and capital planning.

- Provisions and capital: Began incorporating climate factors into PD/LGD via top‑down (macro) and bottom‑up (idiosyncratic) models in Spain, Mexico, Turkey; as of year-end impacts not significant; extraordinary €33m provision for Spain flood events (Oct–Nov 2024).

- Sustainability data strategy: Ongoing gap analysis and process redesign to capture energy efficiency, emissions, ESG, location and sector metrics across products/geographies; leveraging third‑party data, AI on public sources, and enhanced client onboarding; EPC data integration and sector collaboration to standardize transition-risk valuation; sustainability projects embedded in Group’s tech agenda with global indicators.

- Methodologies and standards: Alignment with EU Taxonomy, CSRD/ESRS, ECB/EBA guidance; use of TCFD, UNEP‑FI, ICMA/LMA principles; portfolio alignment and emissions accounting via PACTA/PCAF; NZBA participation; physical risk tools (ThinkHazard/IPCC) and natural capital tools (ENCORE, SBTN). Environmental & Social Framework strengthened with biodiversity/deforestation prohibitions and agro‑sector restrictions; Equator Principles applied with enhanced biodiversity requirements.

structure.title: Social Risk
structure.heading: 7.3. Social Risk
structure.start_phrase: BBVA's sustainability strategy focuses on two central pillars.
structure.summary:
- Focus area: BBVA’s Social Risk disclosures (Pillar 3 2024, Section 7.3.1) on integrating social factors into strategy and business processes, aligned with CRR Article 449 bis Table (2).
- Strategic pillars: (1) Fight against climate change and protect natural capital; (2) Promote inclusive growth.
- Lines of action:
  - Generate quality employment for 125,000+ employees and uphold labor standards.
  - Help customers improve financial health and transition to sustainability through innovation and technology.
  - Support society—especially vulnerable groups—via banks’ and foundations’ social action under the 2025 Community Investment Goal.
- Just transition approach: Assess impacts of climate mitigation/adaptation initiatives on customers, employees, suppliers, communities, and society; design solutions to manage impacts and ensure fairness.
- Inclusive economy initiatives: Finance infrastructure, promote financial inclusion, support entrepreneurs and SMEs; philanthropic programs in education, entrepreneurship, community support, research, and culture within the 2025 Community Investment Goal.
- Targets and progress toward inclusive growth:
  - 2018–2024: EUR 304bn channeled in sustainable business (target of EUR 300bn reached one year early); 78% climate-related, 22% inclusive growth.
- 2024 results by segment:
  - Wholesale clients: ~EUR 51bn sustainable pipeline (+27% YoY); EUR 5bn tied to inclusive growth. Corporate financing and transaction banking: EUR 40bn total, EUR 4bn inclusive growth.
  - Enterprise/corporate clients: EUR 34bn channeled (+62% YoY); EUR 8bn inclusive growth. Corporate financing and transactional banking: EUR 32bn total, EUR 7bn inclusive growth.
- Local initiatives: Launch of a biodiversity bond in Colombia; new sustainability-linked opportunities in the wine sector in Mexico and Spain.
- Volume and capability building:
  - Sustainable operations (loans, confirming, credit lines) nearly tripled YoY to 75,000+; Mexico accounted for 66%+ of operations.
  - Training for managers on sustainability products and digital solutions; structured commercial plans supported by sustainability advisory services.

structure.title: Strategy and business processes
structure.heading: 7.3.1. Strategy and business processes
structure.start_phrase: BBVA's sustainability strategy focuses on two central pillars.
structure.summary:
- Scope: Pillar 3 2024 disclosures on Social Risk (Section 7.3), covering strategy, objectives, business performance, limits/procedures, and risk management integration.
- Strategy: BBVA’s sustainability strategy has two pillars—climate/natural capital and inclusive growth—aiming for positive societal impact via employment, customer financial health and transition support, and targeted social action for vulnerable groups. Emphasis on just transition by assessing stakeholder impacts of climate mitigation/adaptation.
- Inclusive growth solutions: Financing infrastructure, promoting financial inclusion, and supporting entrepreneurs/SMEs; complemented by philanthropic programs in education, entrepreneurship, community support, research, and culture under the 2025 Community Investment Goal.
- Sustainable business goals and progress: 2018–2024 channeling reached EUR 304bn (target EUR 300bn met one year early), with 78% for climate and 22% for inclusive growth.
- 2024 performance by segment:
  - Wholesale clients: ~EUR 51bn channeled (+27% YoY), EUR 5bn linked to inclusive growth; corporate financing/transaction banking EUR 40bn (EUR 4bn inclusive).
  - Enterprise customers: EUR 34bn (+62% YoY), EUR 8bn inclusive; corporate financing/transactional EUR 32bn (EUR 7bn inclusive). Local initiatives include a Colombia biodiversity bond and new business in the wine sector in Mexico and Spain.
  - Retail customers: EUR 14bn channeled (+60% YoY), EUR 9bn inclusive; EUR 6bn specifically for inclusion/consolidation of retail, entrepreneurs and SMEs.
  - Operational metrics: >75,000 sustainable operations closed (nearly tripled YoY), with Mexico accounting for >66%; extensive manager training on sustainable products and digital solutions.
- Financial inclusion outcomes: >280,000 unbanked/underbanked included through accounts, cards, digital payments, and literacy; 3.3 million entrepreneurs/micro-enterprises “bankarized” in 2024 toward a 2018–2025 goal of 4.5 million (4.2 million supported to date); youth financial inclusion initiatives in Spain.
- Community investment: 2021–2025 goal achieved early—EUR 567m invested benefiting ~106 million people (target: EUR 550m and 100m). Key vehicles: BBVA Foundation, BBVA Mexico Foundation (“Chavos que Inspiran”), and BBVA Microfinance Foundation (Colombia, Chile, Panama, Peru, Dominican Republic).
- Limits and procedures for social risk: Environmental and Social Framework sets sector criteria (mining, agribusiness, energy, infrastructure, defense) with prohibited activities (human rights violations incl. child/forced labor and trafficking; projects affecting indigenous peoples without FPIC; controversial weapons and certain nuclear-related activities). Application of Equator Principles (EP4) across project-related products. Internal inclusive growth standard aligned with Human Rights principles, Social Bond Principles, and localized thresholds.
- Risk management framework: Social factors integrated into financial and non-financial risk management, notably via a reputational risk taxonomy tied to ESG expectations. Triggers include misaligned standards, non-credible commitments, onboarding controversial clients, financing contentious activities, green/social-washing, and irresponsible sustainability communications.
- Governance and processes: Annual reputational risk assessments and ongoing admission screening of new initiatives/clients for social controversies, with mitigation plans. Alignment with international standards and initiatives: UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights, ILO conventions, UN SDGs/2030 Agenda, UNEP-FI Principles for Responsible Banking; engagement in UNEP-FI’s Social and Human Rights Thematic Advisory Group.

structure.title: Risk Management
structure.heading: 7.3.2. Risk Management
structure.start_phrase: BBVA is inspired by international industry principles and standards when designing its social risk management framework:
structure.summary:
- Scope and exclusions:
  - Prohibits financing of projects that involve resettlement or infringement of indigenous or vulnerable groups’ rights without Free, Prior and Informed Consent (FPIC).
  - Excludes manufacturers/dealers of controversial weapons (anti-personnel mines, biological/chemical weapons, cluster munitions, depleted uranium, white phosphorus, and nuclear weapons when operating in non-NPT signatory/breaching countries).

- Use of international standards:
  - Applies the Equator Principles (EP4) globally across advisory, project finance, corporate loans, bridge loans, and refinancing/acquisitions.
  - Social risk framework aligned with UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights, SDGs, ILO Conventions, and UNEP-FI Principles for Responsible Banking; participates in UNEP-FI’s Social & Human Rights TAG.
  - Internal inclusive growth standard, aligned with Social Bond Principles and tailored with local methodologies and thresholds.

- Integration of social and reputational risks:
  - Social factors embedded alongside environmental and governance risks, including reputational risk.
  - Reputational risk taxonomy and triggers include misaligned internal standards, non-credible public commitments, onboarding controversial clients, financing controversial operations, mislabeling sustainability, and irresponsible sustainability communications.
  - Annual reputational risk assessment and continuous screening of new initiatives; analysis of clients’ social controversies to prevent/mitigate ESG risks.

- Wholesale client social risk management:
  - Environmental & Social Framework: independent advisor verifies no prohibited activities, flags activities needing enhanced due diligence, and may initiate client dialogue/support plans; by end-2024, 346 groups assessed and five dialogue plans active.
  - ESG integration guide for wholesale credit identifies key E/S issues by industry and defines monitoring metrics.
  - Controversy management procedure (since 2024) integrates E/S controversy scores (impact, risk, management) into client ratings, KYC, and risk appetite across both covered and non-covered clients.

- Equator Principles application and results:
  - Project due diligence covers environmental/human rights impacts; requires FPIC for projects affecting indigenous peoples, community engagement, grievance mechanisms, and climate scenario assessment.
  - Projects categorized A/B/C by impact severity; integrated into structuring, approval, and monitoring with specialist oversight.
  - 2024 operational data (vs. 2023): 81 operations analyzed (54), 62 signed (43), 8 rejected on business/risk grounds (11). Sector split of signed deals: 50% power generation, 44% infrastructure, 6% other; geography: 56% Americas, 44% EMEA.
  - Category totals in 2024: A—5 transactions (€5,366m total; €440m BBVA share); B—40 transactions (€27,079m; €2,943m); C—17 transactions (€21,972m; €1,334m).

- Retail customer social risk:
  - Risk-based KYC to understand customer activity, segmentation, channels, and transaction traceability.
  - Policies ensure non-discrimination in access to credit; admission/pricing models exclude protected attributes (gender, ethnicity, disability, religion, sexual orientation, political opinion).

- Human Rights due diligence and action plans:
  - Two global HRDD exercises since 2018 to prevent, mitigate, and remedy risks (e.g., trafficking/forced labor, child labor, freedom of association/collective bargaining, equal pay, discrimination).
  - Group Human Rights Action Plan published; country-level replications (Spain, Mexico, Turkey, Argentina, Colombia, Peru, Uruguay, Venezuela) with prioritized local issues, semi-annual monitoring, and strengthened procedures.
  - Internal taxonomy of 28 human rights topics in six blocks (employment conditions, projects/products for corporates, supply chain, customer well-being, respect for communities, cross-cutting issues like data protection/technology impacts).
  - For each topic, assesses inherent and residual risk, considering potential impacts on employees (with focus on women), suppliers, customers, indigenous peoples, and local communities.
  - Ongoing tracking of 2021–2023 Human Rights Action Plan progress through 2024.

- Grievance mechanisms:
  - Whistleblower Channel available to all stakeholders, with confidential/anonymous reporting; 2024 cases showed no human rights abuses attributable to BBVA entities.

structure.title: Governance Risk
structure.heading: 7.4. Governance Risk
structure.start_phrase: Governance risks in relation to our counterparties include the various types of controversies they may face, including, but not limited to, the following:
structure.summary:
- Defines governance risk in relation to counterparties and incorporates counterparty governance performance into governance risk disclosures, aligned with Article 449 bis CRR (Table (3) a–d).
- Outlines key governance controversy areas: ethics and anti-bribery/anti-corruption; strategy execution, internal controls and risk management; diversity and inclusion (gender/pay gaps, minority representation in management); transparency on discrimination, tax, and lobbying; management of conflicts of interest; and escalation of critical internal concerns.
- Describes how BBVA integrates counterparty corporate governance into decision-making, assessing operational performance, internal controls, oversight structures, and the quality of financial and non-financial reporting.
- Embeds sustainability governance into KYC/client onboarding, including board-level sustainability oversight and linking sustainability targets to management remuneration, with heightened focus in high-ESG-risk sectors.
- References external frameworks guiding analysis: UN SDGs, UN Global Compact, OECD Guidelines for Multinational Enterprises, PRI, and UNEP-FI Principles for Responsible Banking.
- Explains governance integration into risk management similarly to environmental and social risks, factoring client governance practices into risk underwriting.
- Details incorporation into standard risk, compliance, and operations tools, using internal and external analyst information; governance factors are included in the corporate segment credit rating model’s Governance and Management module.
- Presents BBVA’s risk taxonomy standard, treating governance risks as level-2 risks that map to prudential categories (credit, real estate, market, liquidity and funding, business strategy, operational, reputational), with reputational risk including negative perceptions from third-party associations.
- States that client governance performance and any disputes inform risk appetite and other internal risk indicators.

structure.title: Risk Management
structure.heading: 7.4.1. Risk Management
structure.start_phrase: BBVA builds governance aspects into its risk management framework, much in the same way it does with environmental and social risks.
structure.summary:
- Focus: BBVA’s governance risk approach (Section 7.4), integrating counterparty governance performance into risk assessment in line with Article 449 bis CRR (Table 3 a–d).
- Counterparty governance risk sources: controversies in ethics/anti-bribery/compliance; strategy and risk management/internal controls; diversity and inclusion (gender/pay gaps, minority representation); transparency (discrimination data, tax, lobbying disclosure); conflicts of interest; weak internal escalation of critical issues.
- Decision-making integration: evaluation of internal controls, oversight structures, and quality/assurance of financial and non-financial reporting.
- KYC and onboarding: assessment of sustainability governance, including board-level oversight and linking sustainability targets to management remuneration; heightened scrutiny in high-ESG-risk sectors.
- Reference frameworks: UN SDGs, UN Global Compact, OECD Guidelines for Multinational Enterprises, PRI, and UNEP FI Principles for Responsible Banking.
- Risk management: governance embedded in standard risk, compliance, and operations tools; captured in the Governance & Management module of the corporate credit rating model.
- Risk taxonomy: governance risks classified as level-2 and mapped to prudential categories (credit, real estate, market, liquidity/funding, business strategy, operational, reputational), with reputational risk including negative association with third parties.
- Credit impact: management/governance analysis feeds credit ratings via factors on strategic positioning, financial and risk management, operational efficiency, and governance/reporting practices; acts as a negative modifier when basic governance information is missing; aligned with EBA ESG governance factors.
- Climate governance: review of clients’ integration of climate considerations into governance and decision-making per TCFD.
- Controversy monitoring: analysis of ESG disputes on ethics, transparency/lobbying, and conflicts of interest as indicators of governance quality.
- Annual reviews: verification of internal sustainability/climate committees and integration of sustainability targets into executive remuneration.
- Environmental and Social Framework: independent screening of wholesale clients for prohibited activities; assessment of activities of special attention; potential dialogue/support plans; biennial sector reviews (346 groups assessed by end-2024; five plans active).
- Prohibited activities: no financing for new clients/projects under EU/US/UN sanctions or using child/forced labor (ILO); for existing clients, remediation up to discontinuation of financing.
